vignette:
At 77, Margaret Hale had spent most of her adult life in schools, the kind of counselor who kept peppermint in her desk drawer, remembered siblings' names, and knew how to make an anxious child feel steadier by the end of a lunch period. Widowed for several years, she had continued working part-time at an elementary school, proud that she was still useful and still, as she would have put it before everything changed, "basically a happy person." The event that now divided her life into before and after happened late one afternoon at the school, after the buses had left and the hallways were mostly quiet. A man forced his way into the building during a chaotic confrontation near the front office. Margaret was close enough to hear the shouting, the crash of furniture, and the sudden violent banging that echoed down the corridor. She remembered the metallic slam of the entrance hardware, the sharp report of things being knocked over, and the terrifying uncertainty of not knowing where he was moving next. She and others were rushed into a room and told to stay down and stay silent while the building was secured. What remained fixed in her mind was the sense that an enraged stranger had invaded a place that was supposed to be orderly and safe, and that ordinary sounds in a school could turn, in an instant, into signals of danger.

In the weeks afterward, she found herself listening constantly. At home in the evenings, she would sit in her living room with the television on low, but her attention stayed on the house itself-the creak near the back door, the scrape of a branch against the siding, footsteps she thought she heard on the porch. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home. Even when she checked the locks twice and told herself she was safe, her body would not settle. She startled hard at ordinary noises: the ice maker dropping cubes into the freezer bin, a neighbor shutting a car door, a student knocking unexpectedly on her office door. At school, when children burst laughing into the hallway or a classroom chair screeched across the floor, she jumped in a way that embarrassed her. She began arranging herself close to exits wherever she went. In faculty meetings she chose the chair nearest the door. In the cafeteria during staff development days, she scanned for the fastest way out before she sat down. In her counseling office, she noticed herself angling her chair so she could hear movement in the corridor and leave quickly if she needed to.

Margaret did not describe these habits as excessive. To her, they felt sensible. What frightened her most was how completely she no longer trusted ordinary places. She had come to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing meaningful had been done about it. She returned again and again to thoughts of the man who had entered the school, imagining how to get even with him, rehearsing in her mind what she would say if she ever saw him again, dwelling on the fact that he had taken something from her and gone on existing while she was left with this constant alarm. These thoughts could occupy entire evenings. She would sit with a glass of wine that became two, or take medication to quiet herself enough to get through the night, telling herself she needed something to take the edge off. Sleep did not bring much relief. By morning she often felt dulled and ashamed, then irritated with herself for not being stronger.

Over months, the change in how she saw herself became as painful as the fear. She told her sister that she did not know who she was anymore. This bewildered her almost as much as the original event. She had known herself for decades as calm, warm, and capable in a crisis. Now she felt miserable much of the time and said, with a flat certainty, that she used to be a happy person but was not one now. At school she remained conscientious, but she noticed she was less available to students in the easy, open way that had once defined her. She kept her office door positioned just so, watched the hallway more than she used to, and cut short after-school conversations when the building began to empty. Colleagues saw her as more brittle, and one gently remarked that she seemed tired all the time.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of these daily concessions. After a routine announcement crackled suddenly over the school intercom, she startled so violently in front of a child that the student asked if she was all right. Later that same week, at home, she spent an hour convinced that faint sounds near the side entrance meant someone was trying to get in. Sitting in her kitchen with medication beside her and another drink poured, she realized how small her life had become around doors, sounds, and escape routes. She came to treatment angry, weary, and unconvinced that talking would change what had happened. At the same time, she was hoping for something she could barely say without crying: to feel like herself again, and to be able to sit in a room-at school or in her own home-without waiting for the next sound.
